expectations.text: Zones labeled: the document labels a part for human reading and a separate part for AI-input / archive / evidence material, using explicit headings or banners that name the audience (a bare 'Appendix' does not count), and the two parts do not interleave
expectations.evidence: Near miss. Lines 5-7 are a two-line reader-guide blockquote: 'Dana: §1 and §2 are for you...' / 'Coding agent: read everything. §3 is your brief.' Only two headings name an audience ('## 2. What Dana needs to decide or unblock' and '## 3. Agent brief'). The rest of the agent/archive material sits under bare topic headings ('4. Remaining work, task by task', '5. Reference', '6. Dead ends and gotchas', '7. Assumptions and gaps', '8. Progress log'), which is no better than the bare 'Appendix' the assertion excludes, and the guide tells the agent to 'read everything', so no separate AI/archive zone is delimited or labeled. Order is human first (lines 14-116) then agent (117-387), so nothing interleaves, but the labeling requirement is not met. mechanical.json warns: 'no <!-- zone:... --> markers; human-read and machine/archive content are not marked'.

expectations.text: Human part highlighted: the part written for humans is marked by a prominent banner or heading that says it is for people or where to start (for example an emoji-led 'start here' heading), so a reader cannot miss it
expectations.evidence: Borderline pass. Lines 5-7, directly under the title and purpose line, are the only callout in the document: a blockquote opening '**Dana:** §1 and §2 are for you: where things stand, and the six items that need you.' It names the person and says where to start, and a reader sees it before any section. Weaknesses: it is a plain blockquote rather than an emoji or heading-level banner, it is shared with an instruction for the agent, and the section headings themselves ('1. Where things stand') carry no marker. Passed because the purpose of the assertion, that a human reader cannot miss where to start, is met.

expectations.text: Glance first: the first section after the title is a one-screen overview that states the conclusion itself (what is true or what to do), not merely what the document covers; no background, method or table of contents comes before it

suggestions.assertion: Links work: every in-document link and every image path resolves (scripts/check_doc.py reports no ERROR lines)
suggestions.reason: Passes vacuously for a document with no links. This run has internal_links 0 and no navigation at all, yet check_doc.py reports no ERROR lines. Only the 'Reading path' assertion catches it. Consider requiring a minimum number of resolving section links here, or merging the two.

The run put a two-line reader-guide blockquote under the title naming Dana and the coding agent. The assertions do not say whether a pointer callout counts as a banner, or whether the agent/archive zone needs its own label. I judged 'Human part highlighted' a borderline PASS and 'Zones labeled' a FAIL on the same blockquote. Add a decision rule, for example: each zone must open with a heading or banner that names its audience, and a pointer in the header does not count.

suggestions.assertion: Glance first: the first section after the title is a one-screen overview that states the conclusion itself
suggestions.reason: Mixes 'verdict first' with 'nothing but the verdict before it'. This run states a strong verdict at line 16 but only after 12 lines of purpose, reader guide and provenance bullets, so the outcome turns on how strictly 'no background or method before it' is read. Consider an objective threshold, such as the verdict appearing within the first N lines or before any provenance or marker-legend text.

suggestions.assertion: Dana's view: the first screen says where things stand ... and lists the decisions Dana must make ... with options or a recommendation
suggestions.reason: 'First screen' is defined as the first ~60 lines, but a large image early on pushes the decisions table below the fold when rendered (it sits at lines 48-55, behind a 935 px diagram and an 11-row table). It is also unclear whether each of the five decisions needs an option or recommendation (Q3 and Q5 show '-').

suggestions.assertion: Relationship diagram: ... includes all eleven tasks and draws the dependency edges
suggestions.reason: A diagram with wrong edges would also pass. Consider asserting a few specific edges from tasks.md (T9 fed by exactly T4-T7, T10 by T8 and T9, T11 isolated). This run's edges are all correct, which the current wording cannot distinguish from a wrong one.

No assertion covers how long the human part is. Dana's part (sections 1 and 2) is about 2,100 words and 100 lines with six long question cards, which is a lot for a manager who will 'skim'. A size or collapse requirement would separate a skimmable document from a merely well-ordered one.

No assertion rewards separating source facts from drafting assumptions. This run tags every inference '(assumption)' or '(suggestion)' and lists gaps in section 7, which matters when the agent cannot ask the author. It also caught that 'back 7 Nov' is a Saturday (one working day before the 10 Nov cutover) and that the task list and work log disagree on T7. A hidden-trap check like this would be worth adding.

No assertion checks the loop from Dana back to the agent. This run adds a decision log in section 2 that the agent must act on, and rules for what the agent may do alone versus what needs a named human. That is the core of a dual-audience handoff and is only partly covered by 'Guardrails'.

eval_feedback.overall: Assertions discriminate well on structure (zones, links, headings, diagram), but several depend on undefined thresholds (banner prominence, what counts as the first screen, a link check that passes with zero links), and nothing checks fixture-grounded facts beyond the diagram's nodes. A few fact checks (counts, edges, dates, the Saturday trap) and a length bound on the human part would make the set more discriminating.
